May take with or without food

summary: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation piperazine antihistamine with marked central depressant, anxiolytic, antipruritic, and antiemetic activity. It is used for symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension, for pruritus from allergic conditions such as chronic urticaria and dermatoses, and as a sedative premedication. Sedation is the most common effect, and it carries a risk of dose-related QT prolongation and Torsade de Pointes; it is contraindicated in patients with prolonged QT and in early pregnancy.
indications: Symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension associated with psychoneurosis and as an adjunct in organic disease states with anxiety
Management of pruritus due to allergic conditions such as chronic urticaria and atopic and contact dermatoses
Sedative as premedication and following general anesthesia

dosage.t: Adjust to response; reassess if used beyond 4 months

dosage.n: Children <6 yr: 50 mg daily in divided doses

dosage.d: 25 mg three or four times daily

dosage.n: Children <6 yr: 50 mg daily in divided doses

dosage.t: Single pre-procedure dose; IM may be followed by oral
dosage.n: Reduce concomitant CNS depressant (e.g., meperidine, barbiturate) doses
When initiated IM, subsequent doses may be given orally

admin: May be administered orally with or without food
Oral capsule (hydroxyzine pamoate) is bioequivalent in hydroxyzine content to the hydrochloride salt at the stated mg
For IM use, inject deep into a large muscle; not for IV, intra-arterial, or subcutaneous administration
When premedication is started by IM route, subsequent doses may be switched to oral
Start at the low end of the dosing range in elderly patients and observe closely
Adjust dose to the individual patient's clinical response
moa: Hydroxyzine is a piperazine-derivative competitive antagonist at peripheral and central H1 histamine receptors. Its anxiolytic and sedative effects are thought to result from suppression of activity in subcortical regions of the CNS rather than cortical depression. It also has skeletal muscle relaxant, bronchodilator, analgesic, antiemetic, and mild antisecretory/anticholinergic actions demonstrated experimentally and clinically.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to hydroxyzine or any component
Known hypersensitivity to cetirizine or levocetirizine
relative: Risk factors for QT prolongation / TdP (heart disease, electrolyte imbalance, bradyarrhythmia, recent MI, uncompensated heart failure)
Congenital or family history of long QT syndrome
monitor: ECG/QT in patients with cardiac risk factors or on QT-prolonging drugs
Signs of AGEP or hypersensitivity skin reactions

preg: Contraindicated in early pregnancy. Hydroxyzine induced fetal abnormalities in rats and mice at doses substantially above the human therapeutic range, and human data are inadequate to establish first-trimester safety.
lact: It is not known whether hydroxyzine is excreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in milk, hydroxyzine should not be given to nursing mothers.
renal: The extent of renal excretion has not been fully determined; however, dose reduction or interval extension is advised in renal impairment, and caution is recommended in elderly patients who more often have reduced renal function.
hepatic: Hydroxyzine undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism; reduce the dose in patients with hepatic impairment and start cautiously in the elderly who may have decreased hepatic function.

major: Class IA antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide) - additive QT prolongation
Class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol) - additive QT prolongation
QT-prolonging antipsychotics (ziprasidone, iloperidone, clozapine, quetiapine, chlorpromazine)
QT-prolonging antibiotics (azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin, gatifloxacin, moxifloxacin)
Other QT-prolonging agents (pentamidine, methadone, ondansetron, droperidol)
moderate: CNS depressants - narcotics, non-narcotic analgesics, barbiturates (reduce their dose; hydroxyzine potentiates them)
Meperidine and barbiturates used in pre-anesthetic adjunctive therapy (potentiated)
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to food.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; hydroxyzine increases the CNS-depressant effect of alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: May suppress wheal/flare response in allergy skin testing; discontinue several days before testing. Can also interfere with QT interpretation due to its own QT-prolonging effect.

common: Drowsiness (usually transitory, may resolve with continued therapy or dose reduction)
serious: Convulsions (usually at doses higher than recommended)
emergency: Torsade de Pointes / life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia

monitoring: ECG/QT interval in patients with cardiac risk factors or on QT-prolonging drugs
Serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) in at-risk patients
Level of sedation, especially in elderly
Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion)
Skin for signs of AGEP or hypersensitivity
Periodic reassessment of continued need when used for anxiety beyond 4 months
counsel: May cause marked drowsiness; do not drive or operate dangerous machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol and other sedating drugs while taking this medication
Tell your doctor about any heart rhythm problems or family history of long QT syndrome
Seek urgent care for palpitations, fainting, or a widespread blistering/pustular rash
Dry mouth is common; sugar-free gum or sips of water can help
Do not use if you are or may be pregnant in early pregnancy
Inform clinicians you take hydroxyzine before allergy skin testing
pk: Clinical effect within 15-30 minutes of oral dose
About 20 hours in adults (longer in elderly, ~29 h)
Sedative/antihistaminic effect 4-6 hours, up to 24 h
Store at 20-25C (68-77F); protect from moisture; keep tightly closed
pearls: Useful adjunct antihistamine for chronic urticaria and histamine-mediated pruritus when sedation is acceptable
Dose-related QT prolongation is a class concern; avoid in long QT and stack-check other QT-prolonging drugs
Pamoate (Vistaril) and hydrochloride (Atarax) salts are dosed by equivalent hydroxyzine content
Do NOT use epinephrine to treat hydroxyzine-induced hypotension - hydroxyzine counteracts its pressor effect; use other vasopressors
Strongly anticholinergic - use cautiously in elderly per Beers criteria (confusion, falls, urinary retention)
Often used off-label as a non-dependence-forming option for short-term anxiety and as an antiemetic/premedication
missed: If taking on a scheduled basis, take the missed dose as soon as remembered; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not double up. For as-needed (pruritus/anxiety) use, simply take when symptoms occur.
overdose: The most common manifestation is hypersedation; convulsions, stupor, nausea, and vomiting may occur. Consider gastric lavage if recent and airway protected. Provide general supportive care with frequent vital-sign monitoring. Treat hypotension with IV fluids and vasopressors but NOT epinephrine (hydroxyzine reverses its pressor action). Obtain ECG monitoring because overdose may cause QT prolongation and Torsade de Pointes. There is no specific antidote; hemodialysis is not expected to be helpful unless co-ingested agents (e.g., barbiturates) warrant it.
